IceBrick · intraday PUE optimization · IceBrick 8760 method on measured hours

IT Capacity IceBrick Simulator for DataBank – IAD1 North Virginia

Working out the weather-driven chiller load from the meter data…

Calibrating against the meter data…

IceBrick sizing

The store size is the one input. The charging plant is sized to refill the store in one charge window (store × round-trip loss ÷ window hours). The discharge heat exchanger is sized to the busiest discharge hour the dispatch asks for. Both are in the installed cost per ton-hour. The suggested store sits at the knee of the size curve, where the IT freed per added ton-hour drops by more than 30% from one step to the next. Past that point, one night's refill no longer covers the hardest cycle. RT (refrigeration tons) = 3.517 kWth (kilowatts thermal). Store sizes are in ton-hours banked, before the ×1.08 round-trip loss.

The new IT and what it brings

The freed capacity, filled. Each new kW of IT brings its non-chiller ancillary and its own heat, which the existing chillers carry at their efficiency in every hour. IceBrick then holds the whole filled site at today's peak. All figures follow the store size.

Night-to-day cycles at the peak

Each cycle is one night followed by the next day, starting when the charge window opens. The night banks exactly what the next afternoon will discharge, times the 1.08 round-trip loss, and fills the flattest valleys first. A store bigger than one night can bank ahead of a heat wave and carry ice into the next cycle. Every cycle is held to the same ceiling, so the store is sized by the cycle with the most energy above that ceiling (marked "sizes the store"), which is not always the cycle with the highest peak. Below, the two event days on the same scales: the maximum-demand cycle and the cycle that uses the full store. Pick any other cycle in the table to add it as a third panel.

Facility demand with and without IceBrick, every hour

The same dispatch across the whole period. Light blue is chiller load moved off the afternoon, valued at the plant's own efficiency that hour. Pink is what that move earns on top: the chillers still running sit lower on their part-load curve, and IceBrick post-cools them, so they work at a lower lift. Dark blue is IceBrick's own charging plant at night. It is a separate, colder circuit, so the night has no pink. Meter against BMS, summer 2026

The same IceBrick method and the same store, run on the same hours from two sources: the meter roll-up this simulator is built on, and the BMS (building management system) facility total from the trend export. A third run uses the BMS total with IT taken from the BMS IT reading instead of inferred. The window is the clean part of the BMS export, May 21 to Aug 11, 2026. After that a BMS project distorts its power readings, and the meter file ends on Aug 26. Each source sets its own ceiling from its own peak. Design-day check

The hottest day in the last N years at Dulles, from the ERA5 (European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts fifth reanalysis) record the 8760 simulator uses. It runs as three cycles, the day before through the day after, on the same fitted model and the same IceBrick size. The measured window only saw its own summers, so this asks whether the freed capacity survives a hotter one.

Design day

Calibration: what the meter says the chillers draw

Site demand rises with outdoor temperature only because the chiller plant works harder. Holding each week's load and each hour-of-day pattern fixed, this is the extra demand at each temperature. Dots are the meter data averaged per 2 °F; the line is the fit the dispatch uses.
